stem: A patient with acute anterior STEMI presents to a hospital without PCI facilities; the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI-mediated reperfusion at a transfer centre is 180 minutes. Symptoms began 2 hours ago. What is the recommended strategy?

options.A: Wait for troponin results before deciding
options.C: Medical therapy alone, with elective coronary angiography at 2 weeks
options.D: Fibrinolysis within 10 minutes, then transfer for angiography
options.E: Transfer for primary PCI regardless of delay

explanation: ESC 2023 recommends primary PCI if it can be performed within 120 minutes of diagnosis; otherwise fibrinolysis should be given within 10 minutes of diagnosis in patients without contraindications, with transfer to a PCI centre (rescue PCI if failed reperfusion; routine angiography within 2–24 hours if successful).
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient with ongoing chest pain has horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves. What is the next most useful step?

options.B: Record posterior leads V7–V9 to look for posterior STEMI
options.D: Diagnose NSTEMI and plan angiography within 72 hours of admission
options.E: Give thrombolysis immediately without further ECG

explanation: ST depression in V1–V3 may represent the mirror image of posterior ST elevation from circumflex or right coronary occlusion. ST elevation of ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9 confirms posterior STEMI, which requires emergency reperfusion.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient with inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive after sublingual nitroglycerin. Lungs are clear and the JVP is raised. ST elevation is present in V4R. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.C: Intra-aortic balloon pump as first-line therapy for right ventricular failure
options.D: Cautious IV fluids, avoiding nitrates and diuretics, plus urgent reperfusion

explanation: RV infarction causes preload-dependent hypotension with clear lung fields and raised JVP. Nitrates, diuretics and vasodilators worsen hypotension. Management includes reperfusion, careful fluids, maintaining AV synchrony and inotropes if needed.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: Five days after an inferior MI, a patient develops acute pulmonary oedema and hypotension with a new soft apical systolic murmur. Echocardiography shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet. What is the definitive treatment?

options.A: Urgent surgical mitral repair or replacement, with temporary mechanical support
options.C: Medical therapy alone with diuretics and afterload reduction, then review at 6 weeks

explanation: Papillary muscle rupture (more often posteromedial, supplied by a single artery, typically the RCA) causes acute severe MR and cardiogenic shock. The murmur may be soft because of rapid pressure equalisation. Afterload reduction and IABP or other mechanical support are bridges to urgent surgery.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient with recent anterior MI develops a new harsh pansystolic murmur and shock. Pulmonary artery catheter oxygen saturations are: right atrium 62%, right ventricle 84%, pulmonary artery 85%. What is the diagnosis?

options.D: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture

explanation: An oxygen saturation step-up of more than 5–7% between the right atrium and right ventricle indicates a left-to-right shunt at ventricular level. Post-infarction VSD requires mechanical circulatory support and surgical or percutaneous closure; mortality is very high without repair.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: Which patient with NSTE-ACS requires an immediate invasive strategy (within 2 hours)?

options.A: A patient with refractory recurrent chest pain and haemodynamic instability
options.B: A patient with chronic stable angina
options.C: A patient with a normal ECG and troponin
options.D: A patient with GRACE score of 90 and no symptoms
options.E: A stable patient with a modest troponin rise and no ongoing chest pain at present

explanation: ESC 2023 recommends an immediate invasive strategy for very high-risk NSTE-ACS: haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, recurrent or refractory pain, life-threatening arrhythmias, mechanical complications, acute heart failure clearly related to ACS, or recurrent dynamic ST changes. High-risk patients undergo early angiography within 24 hours.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient with chest pain has upsloping ST depression at the J point in V1–V6 with tall, symmetrical T waves and no ST elevation. What does this pattern suggest?

options.D: Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain and repolarisation changes
options.E: De Winter T waves, a STEMI equivalent of proximal LAD occlusion

explanation: De Winter T waves (up-sloping ST depression with tall symmetrical T waves in precordial leads) are associated with acute proximal LAD occlusion and should be managed as a STEMI equivalent with immediate reperfusion.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient whose chest pain has resolved has deep symmetrical T-wave inversion in V2–V3 with minimal troponin rise. What is the appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge with outpatient follow-up and a stress echocardiogram in about 4 weeks' time
options.C: Exercise stress test the same day
options.E: Early angiography without stress testing; this suggests critical proximal LAD stenosis

explanation: Wellens syndrome (biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3 during pain-free periods) indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis with high risk of anterior MI. Stress testing is contraindicated; early angiography is recommended.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient presents with BP 210/120 mmHg, severe dyspnoea, SpO2 84% and bilateral crackles. Which combination is most appropriate?

options.B: High-dose IV nitrates, NIV and an IV loop diuretic
options.C: Immediate intubation without vasodilators or diuretics

explanation: Hypertensive acute heart failure (sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema) is driven by afterload and fluid redistribution. High-dose nitrates rapidly reduce preload and afterload, NIV improves oxygenation and work of breathing, and diuretics treat volume overload. Morphine is associated with worse outcomes.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]

stem: Two hours after an IV loop diuretic dose in acute heart failure, spot urine sodium is 35 mmol/L. What is the recommended next step according to ESC guidance?

options.B: Start an ACE inhibitor at high dose
options.C: Double the IV loop diuretic dose, as natriuresis is inadequate
options.D: Stop diuretics because the patient is probably intravascularly dehydrated
options.E: Continue the same dose unchanged for 48 hours

explanation: ESC 2021 recommends assessing diuretic response with spot urine sodium after 2 hours (target above 50–70 mmol/L) or urine output in the first 6 hours (above 100–150 mL/h). An inadequate response prompts doubling the loop diuretic dose and then sequential nephron blockade.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: What did the ADVOR trial show regarding acetazolamide in acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload?

options.B: Acetazolamide replaced the need for loop diuretics in most patients with overload
options.C: Acetazolamide was ineffective in all patients
options.D: Adding acetazolamide to loop diuretics improved decongestion within 3 days

explanation: ADVOR randomised 519 patients; IV acetazolamide 500 mg daily added to loop diuretics improved successful decongestion (42.2% vs 30.5%) and natriuresis, without significant differences in death or readmission.
referenceText: Mullens et al. 2022 (ADVOR) [143]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: In infarct-related cardiogenic shock, what did the OptimaCC trial show when comparing adrenaline with noradrenaline?

options.B: Adrenaline improved cardiac index without any adverse metabolic or arrhythmic effects
options.C: Adrenaline reduced mortality compared with noradrenaline
options.D: Both drugs had identical effects on lactate
options.E: Adrenaline caused more refractory shock and higher lactate, stopping the trial early

explanation: OptimaCC was stopped early because adrenaline was associated with higher incidence of refractory cardiogenic shock, higher heart rate and lactate, despite similar effects on cardiac index and MAP. Noradrenaline is generally preferred when a vasopressor is needed in cardiogenic shock.
referenceText: Levy et al. 2018 (OptimaCC) [129]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: A patient with severe LV systolic dysfunction (EF 25%) develops AF with ventricular rate 150/min and BP 98/60 mmHg. Which drug is most appropriate for acute rate control?
explanation: In AF with reduced LVEF or haemodynamic compromise, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are avoided because of negative inotropy. Digoxin and/or amiodarone are preferred; electrical cardioversion is indicated for haemodynamic instability.
referenceText: Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]

stem: A stable patient has AF of uncertain duration and is not anticoagulated. Elective cardioversion is planned. What is required before cardioversion?

options.B: No anticoagulation is needed if the CHA2DS2-VA score is zero and the AF began recently
options.D: Three weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE exclusion of left atrial thrombus

explanation: ESC guidance recommends 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation before cardioversion of AF lasting more than 24–48 hours or of unknown duration, or imaging to exclude left atrial thrombus. Anticoagulation should continue for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion.
referenceText: Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]

stem: A patient develops new-onset AF at 130/min during septic shock on noradrenaline. MAP is 68 mmHg. Which statement about management is most appropriate?

options.C: Treat sepsis and electrolytes; use rate or rhythm control cautiously, often amiodarone
options.D: Ignore the arrhythmia, because new AF never affects haemodynamics in septic shock patients
options.E: Elective cardioversion after 3 weeks of anticoagulation

explanation: New AF in sepsis is common and often resolves with treatment of the underlying illness, electrolyte correction and reduction in catecholamines. Amiodarone is often chosen because of less hypotension; beta-blockers such as esmolol or landiolol are used in selected patients. Anticoagulation decisions are individualised.
referenceText: Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: In the 2024 ESC AF guideline, which stroke risk score is recommended?
explanation: The 2024 ESC guideline uses the CHA2DS2-VA score (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 [2 points], diabetes, stroke/TIA/thromboembolism [2 points], vascular disease, age 65–74), removing female sex. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for a score of 2 or more and should be considered for a score of 1.
referenceText: Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]

stem: Which ECG feature in a broad-complex tachycardia most strongly supports ventricular tachycardia over SVT with aberrancy?

options.B: Atrioventricular dissociation with capture or fusion beats
options.E: Typical right bundle branch block morphology in V1

explanation: AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats are highly specific for VT. Other features include very broad QRS (above 160 ms), extreme axis deviation and concordance in precordial leads. In patients with structural heart disease, broad-complex tachycardia should be treated as VT until proven otherwise.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]

stem: CT angiography shows an aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta. What is the classification and the treatment of choice?

options.B: Stanford type A; medical therapy and repeat imaging
options.C: Stanford type B; medical therapy alone
options.E: Stanford type B; thoracic endovascular repair in all cases

explanation: Any dissection involving the ascending aorta (Stanford A, DeBakey I and II) requires emergency surgery because of the risk of rupture, tamponade, aortic regurgitation and coronary malperfusion. Uncomplicated type B dissections are managed medically, while complicated type B dissections receive endovascular repair.
referenceText: Mazzolai et al. 2024 (ESC peripheral arterial and aortic diseases) [133]

stem: A patient with acute type B aortic dissection has BP 185/105 mmHg and heart rate 105/min. What is the initial pharmacological approach?

options.C: IV sodium nitroprusside alone as the first agent, before any beta-blocker is started
options.E: IV beta-blocker first (e.g. esmolol), aiming HR <60/min and SBP 100–120 mmHg

explanation: Reducing the rate of rise of aortic pressure (dP/dt) and wall stress is the goal. Beta-blockade comes first to prevent reflex tachycardia, then vasodilators are added. ESC targets a heart rate below 60/min and systolic BP below 120 mmHg, with adequate analgesia.
referenceText: Mazzolai et al. 2024 (ESC peripheral arterial and aortic diseases) [133]

stem: A patient with hypertensive encephalopathy has BP 230/130 mmHg. What is the recommended blood pressure reduction?

options.A: Lower MAP by ≤25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100–110 mmHg over 2–6 hours
options.C: Normalise blood pressure to 120/80 mmHg within 30 minutes using IV labetalol boluses
options.D: Reduce systolic BP by 50% within 15 minutes

explanation: In hypertensive emergencies without compelling conditions, BP should be reduced by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100–110 mmHg over 2–6 hours and towards normal over 24–48 hours. Rapid normalisation risks cerebral, coronary and renal ischaemia. Aortic dissection, severe pre-eclampsia and phaeochromocytoma crisis require faster targets.
referenceText: Whelton et al. 2018 (ACC/AHA hypertension) [235]

stem: A patient with suspected phaeochromocytoma has paroxysmal BP 260/140 mmHg with tachycardia. Which drug should be given first?

options.D: An alpha-adrenergic antagonist such as phentolamine
options.E: Metoprolol followed by phenoxybenzamine after 1 week

explanation: In catecholamine excess, beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening hypertension and causing heart failure. Phentolamine (IV) or other alpha-blockers come first; beta-blockers are added for tachycardia after alpha-blockade.
referenceText: Whelton et al. 2018 (ACC/AHA hypertension) [235]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A 30-year-old man has chest pain, agitation, tachycardia and hypertension after cocaine use. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.B: Benzodiazepines, adding nitrates or calcium channel blockers
options.C: Thrombolysis in all patients presenting with chest pain after cocaine use

explanation: Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate and BP. Nitrates and calcium channel blockers treat hypertension and coronary vasospasm. Non-selective beta-blockers have traditionally been avoided because of unopposed alpha stimulation. ST elevation is treated with primary PCI.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]; Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: Which echocardiographic sign is most specific for haemodynamically significant pericardial tamponade?

options.A: Collapsing inferior vena cava with inspiration
options.D: Small pericardial effusion without chamber collapse

explanation: Tamponade causes right atrial systolic collapse (sensitive) and right ventricular diastolic collapse (more specific), a plethoric IVC without respiratory variation, and exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral (above 25%) and tricuspid inflow velocities. Diagnosis remains clinical and haemodynamic.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: A postmenopausal woman develops chest pain, ST elevation and apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis after severe emotional stress. Coronary angiography shows no obstruction. Which management is important if she becomes hypotensive?

options.A: Check for LVOT obstruction; if present, avoid inotropes and use fluids and beta-blockers
options.C: High-dose dobutamine in all cases, to support the failing apical segments until recovery

explanation: Takotsubo syndrome is a reversible stress cardiomyopathy with apical ballooning. About 20% develop dynamic LVOT obstruction due to basal hypercontractility; catecholamines worsen it. Levosimendan or mechanical support are options in cardiogenic shock without obstruction.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A patient with Staphylococcus aureus mitral valve endocarditis has a 14-mm mobile vegetation and a recent splenic embolus despite appropriate antibiotics. What is the recommended management?

options.B: Add thrombolysis to dissolve the vegetation
options.C: Urgent surgery to prevent further embolism

explanation: ESC 2023 recommends urgent surgery for persistent vegetations of 10 mm or more after one or more embolic episodes despite appropriate antibiotics. Other indications include heart failure from valve dysfunction (emergency if cardiogenic shock) and uncontrolled infection (abscess, persisting bacteraemia).
referenceText: Delgado et al. 2023 (ESC infective endocarditis) [51]

stem: A patient with native valve endocarditis develops an acute ischaemic stroke. Which therapy is contraindicated?

options.D: Early cardiac surgery if indicated and no intracranial haemorrhage

explanation: Thrombolysis is not recommended in endocarditis-related stroke because of high risk of intracranial haemorrhage (septic arteritis, mycotic aneurysms). Mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in selected patients; surgery is generally not delayed after ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage and with preserved consciousness.
referenceText: Delgado et al. 2023 (ESC infective endocarditis) [51]; Powers et al. 2019 (AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke) [168]

stem: A patient with severe aortic stenosis develops hypotension after induction of anaesthesia. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Phenylephrine or noradrenaline to restore diastolic and coronary perfusion pressure
options.E: Dobutamine infusion to increase heart rate and cardiac output across the stenotic aortic valve

explanation: In severe AS, cardiac output is fixed; vasodilatation drops coronary perfusion pressure in a hypertrophied ventricle, causing ischaemia and a downward spiral. Alpha agonists, adequate preload, avoidance of tachycardia and maintenance of sinus rhythm are key.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with aortic valve endocarditis develops acute severe aortic regurgitation with pulmonary oedema and hypotension. Which intervention is contraindicated?
explanation: IABP inflation in diastole increases regurgitant volume and is contraindicated in significant aortic regurgitation. Acute severe AR is a surgical emergency; inotropes and vasodilators are bridges, and relative tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces regurgitation.
referenceText: Delgado et al. 2023 (ESC infective endocarditis) [51]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: Which patient most needs temporary transvenous pacing?

options.B: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) block during sleep in an athlete
options.D: Sinus bradycardia at 52/min in a patient on beta-blockers with a normal blood pressure
options.E: Complete heart block with broad escape, syncope and compromise unresponsive to drugs

explanation: Temporary pacing is indicated for symptomatic high-grade AV block, especially with broad escape rhythms, or bradycardia unresponsive to drugs. Mobitz I and first-degree block rarely require pacing; asymptomatic sinus bradycardia does not.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: Which is a recognised acute adverse effect of IV amiodarone in critically ill patients?

options.A: Rapid onset pulmonary fibrosis within hours in most patients

explanation: IV amiodarone causes hypotension (partly from the solvent polysorbate 80) and bradycardia, and may cause phlebitis and acute hepatotoxicity. Pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction and other organ effects are usually associated with long-term use, although acute pulmonary toxicity is described.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with septic shock has a troponin rise above the 99th percentile without ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes. How is this best classified?

options.A: Type 1 MI requiring immediate coronary angiography and loading with dual antiplatelets
options.C: Non-ischaemic myocardial injury, or possibly type 2 MI from supply–demand imbalance

explanation: The fourth universal definition distinguishes myocardial injury (troponin above the 99th percentile) from MI (injury plus evidence of acute ischaemia). In sepsis, troponin elevation commonly reflects injury or type 2 MI and is associated with mortality but does not usually require urgent angiography.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: What is the most common ECG finding in acute pulmonary embolism?

options.E: Right axis deviation in all cases

explanation: Sinus tachycardia is the most frequent ECG finding in PE. S1Q3T3, right bundle branch block, T inversion in V1–V4 and right axis deviation suggest RV strain but are insensitive and non-specific.
referenceText: Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]

stem: Which ECG finding is characteristic of moderate to severe hypothermia?

options.A: Osborn (J) waves at the QRS–ST junction
options.D: Shortened QT interval with peaked T waves

explanation: Osborn or J waves are positive deflections at the J point, more prominent with lower temperatures. Other features include bradycardia, prolonged intervals, AF and, below about 28 °C, a risk of VF. Rough handling may precipitate VF.
referenceText: Brown et al. 2012 (accidental hypothermia) [27]

stem: A febrile patient has coved ST elevation of 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in V1–V2. What is the significance?

options.C: Type 1 Brugada pattern unmasked by fever, with arrhythmic risk; treat fever
options.E: Anterior STEMI requiring immediate thrombolysis or primary PCI within 90 minutes

explanation: Fever can unmask a type 1 Brugada ECG pattern caused by sodium channel dysfunction, increasing the risk of polymorphic VT/VF. Antipyretics, avoidance of sodium channel blockers and monitoring are required; isoprenaline or quinidine treat electrical storm.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]

stem: Which combination most increases the risk of torsades de pointes in an ICU patient?

options.A: Normal electrolytes and a single QT-neutral drug at standard dose
options.C: Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and QT-prolonging drugs

explanation: Risk factors for drug-induced torsades include female sex, bradycardia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, structural heart disease and multiple QT-prolonging drugs (antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, methadone, antiarrhythmics). Daily ECG and electrolyte monitoring help prevent it.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: Which measure reduces postoperative AF after cardiac surgery?

options.B: Perioperative beta-blockers or amiodarone prophylaxis in high-risk patients
options.D: Routine calcium channel blockers in all patients after cardiopulmonary bypass

explanation: Postoperative AF occurs in about 30% of patients after cardiac surgery. Continuing or starting beta-blockers, amiodarone prophylaxis and correcting potassium and magnesium reduce its incidence. Posterior pericardiotomy has also been shown to reduce postoperative AF.
referenceText: Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Six hours after CABG, a patient has low cardiac index, rising CVP and wedge pressure, falling urine output and increasing chest drain output that suddenly stops. What diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
explanation: Postoperative tamponade may be localised and does not always show classic signs; sudden cessation of drainage with haemodynamic deterioration suggests clotted drains. Echocardiography (often transoesophageal) helps, but clinical suspicion should prompt re-exploration.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: A young adult presents with viral prodrome, cardiogenic shock, ventricular arrhythmias and severe global LV dysfunction with normal coronary arteries. What is the most appropriate supportive strategy?

options.B: Early transfer for mechanical circulatory support, with endomyocardial biopsy
options.D: Exercise testing to stratify arrhythmic risk before discharge on oral therapy

explanation: Fulminant myocarditis can recover fully if patients survive the acute phase with mechanical support (VA-ECMO, Impella). Endomyocardial biopsy identifies giant cell or eosinophilic myocarditis, which respond to immunosuppression. NSAIDs may worsen myocarditis in the acute phase.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy becomes hypotensive during sepsis. Which drug is most likely to worsen the outflow obstruction?
explanation: Inotropes and vasodilators increase LVOT obstruction by increasing contractility and reducing LV volume. Management involves fluids, pure vasoconstrictors and beta-blockers to slow heart rate and prolong diastolic filling.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve and subtherapeutic INR presents with acute pulmonary oedema and muffled valve clicks. Echocardiography shows obstructive prosthetic valve thrombosis. What is the preferred treatment if surgery is immediately available and the patient is not high risk?

options.E: Observation and repeat echocardiography in 1 week

explanation: For obstructive left-sided mechanical valve thrombosis in critically ill patients, urgent surgery is recommended when available and operative risk is acceptable; fibrinolysis is an alternative when surgery is unavailable or high risk.
referenceText: Delgado et al. 2023 (ESC infective endocarditis) [51]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis in STEMI?

options.B: Systolic BP of 165 mmHg on admission that responds to treatment
options.E: Known structural cerebral vascular lesion such as an arteriovenous malformation

explanation: Absolute contraindications include previous intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke in the previous 6 months, CNS tumour or vascular malformation, recent major trauma, surgery or head injury (within 1 month), GI bleeding within 1 month, known bleeding disorder, aortic dissection and non-compressible punctures in the past 24 hours.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: In cardiogenic shock, what does a cardiac power output below 0.6 W indicate?
explanation: Cardiac power output = MAP × CO / 451 (in W) integrates pressure and flow. In the SHOCK registry, it was the strongest haemodynamic predictor of mortality in cardiogenic shock, with values below 0.6 W associated with poor outcomes.
referenceText: Naidu et al. 2022 (SCAI shock stages) [146]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: What is the current ESC position on routine morphine use in acute heart failure?

options.A: Recommended as first-line therapy for pulmonary oedema
options.B: Recommended in all patients to reduce preload
options.C: Contraindicated in all circumstances, including palliation of breathlessness at the end of life
options.D: Recommended at high doses to reduce sympathetic drive
options.E: Not recommended routinely, except selected patients with severe pain or anxiety

explanation: ESC 2021 does not recommend routine opiates in acute heart failure; observational data link morphine to more mechanical ventilation, ICU admission and mortality. Opiates may be used cautiously for severe pain or anxiety, or in palliative care.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

stem: A 38-year-old woman 3 weeks postpartum presents with NSTEMI. Angiography shows a long smooth narrowing in the mid LAD without atherosclerosis, and she is stable with TIMI 3 flow. What is the preferred management?

options.B: Immediate stenting of the entire dissected segment
options.C: Conservative medical therapy, as most cases heal

explanation: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection affects young women, particularly peripartum. In stable patients with preserved flow, conservative management is preferred because PCI has higher complication rates and most dissections heal. Thrombolysis may extend the haematoma and is avoided.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: Which ECG finding best supports acute pericarditis rather than STEMI?

options.A: Convex ST elevation in a coronary territory with reciprocal ST depression
options.B: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, without reciprocal changes
options.D: Q waves in leads II, III and aVF

explanation: Pericarditis causes widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression with reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation only in aVR (and V1), without Q waves. Regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes suggests infarction.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: A patient with cardiogenic shock from dilated cardiomyopathy has cold, wet peripheries with MAP 72 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.05 µg/kg/min and low cardiac index. Which drug is most appropriate to add to improve cardiac output?
explanation: Inotropes such as dobutamine (or milrinone, levosimendan) are used to improve cardiac output in patients with hypoperfusion despite adequate filling. Phenylephrine and high-dose vasopressors increase afterload without improving contractility, and beta-blockers are contraindicated in shock.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Naidu et al. 2022 (SCAI shock stages) [146]

stem: A patient with acute type B aortic dissection develops abdominal pain, rising lactate and acute kidney injury. What is the best management?

options.B: Thrombolysis for presumed embolic mesenteric ischaemia
options.E: TEVAR, because the dissection is complicated by malperfusion

explanation: Complicated type B dissection (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension, rapid expansion) requires urgent intervention, preferably TEVAR to cover the primary entry tear, restoring true lumen flow.
referenceText: Mazzolai et al. 2024 (ESC peripheral arterial and aortic diseases) [133]

stem: For most patients with ACS undergoing PCI without high bleeding risk, what is the default antiplatelet regimen?

options.A: Aspirin plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (prasugrel or ticagrelor) for 12 months
options.D: Triple therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel and rivaroxaban for 12 months

explanation: ESC 2023 recommends dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and prasugrel or ticagrelor for 12 months as default after ACS, unless there is high bleeding risk; clopidogrel is used when potent agents are contraindicated or with oral anticoagulants. De-escalation strategies are options in selected patients.
referenceText: Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

subtopic: flash with bilateral renal artery stenosis
stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of flash pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, preserved ejection fraction and worsening renal function after starting an ACE inhibitor. What diagnosis should be considered?
explanation: Flash pulmonary oedema with hypertension and AKI after ACE inhibition suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis (Pickering syndrome). Revascularisation may be considered in recurrent flash oedema.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]
tags: flash with bilateral renal artery stenosis

stem: A patient with acute heart failure has cold peripheries, low blood pressure and no signs of congestion after diuresis. In the clinical profile classification (warm/cold, wet/dry), which profile is this and what does it imply?

options.A: The classification does not apply to acute heart failure; it is used only for chronic disease
options.B: Warm and wet; requiring vasodilators and diuretics
options.C: Cold and dry; hypoperfusion without congestion, needing volume assessment, not diuretics
options.D: Cold and wet; requiring high-dose diuretics only
options.E: Warm and dry; compensated, requiring no change

explanation: The bedside haemodynamic profile combines perfusion (warm/cold) and congestion (wet/dry). Cold–dry patients may be over-diuresed or have very low output; further diuresis worsens hypoperfusion. Cold–wet patients need inotropes or vasopressors plus decongestion; warm–wet patients need vasodilators and diuretics.
referenceText: McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]
